title: Dynamic Programming
tagline: The technique that transforms exponential brute-force into polynomial solutions by never solving the same subproblem twice.

sections.content:
Dynamic programming (DP) is not a single algorithm — it is a **design technique** that applies whenever a problem can be broken into overlapping subproblems whose solutions combine to form the solution to the whole. Recognising the pattern is the skill: once you see it, an exponential brute-force search collapses to a polynomial (often O(n²) or O(n·W)) computation.

The two hallmarks of a DP problem are **overlapping subproblems** (the same sub-computation is needed many times) and **optimal substructure** (the optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems). Classic examples include Fibonacci, coin change, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, and edit distance — each appears repeatedly in technical interviews and real systems (compilers, route planning, NLP).

sections.title: Climbing Stairs With a Notepad
sections.content:
Imagine counting the distinct ways to climb n stairs, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. A naïve approach tries every path: from stair n you could have come from n-1 (one step) or n-2 (two steps), and you recurse on each. For stair 40 this fans out into millions of redundant calls.

Now bring a notepad. The first time you compute 'ways to reach stair k', you write it down. Every subsequent call for stair k reads from the notepad instead of recursing. The notebook is your **memo table** — this is memoisation. The alternative is to fill the notepad left-to-right from stair 0 upward, without any recursion at all — this is **tabulation**. Both eliminate redundancy; they differ only in direction (top-down vs bottom-up).

**Overlapping subproblems** is the defining characteristic. In plain recursion for Fibonacci, `fib(5)` calls `fib(4)` and `fib(3)`; `fib(4)` also calls `fib(3)` — the `fib(3)` subtree is computed twice (and exponentially more redundancy grows deeper). Memoisation (top-down DP) attaches a cache to the recursion: before computing `fib(n)`, check if the answer is cached; if so, return it immediately. The recursion tree collapses from exponential to linear — each value is computed exactly once.

**Optimal substructure** means the global optimum is built from subproblem optima. Coin change asks: what is the minimum number of coins summing to amount W? The recurrence is `dp[w] = 1 + min(dp[w - coin])` for each coin ≤ w. The optimal solution for amount w uses the optimal solution for amount `w - coin` — you do not need to know *which* specific coins were used for `w - coin`, only the minimum count. This composability is what makes DP possible.

**Memoisation (top-down)** wraps an existing recursive solution with a cache. It computes only the subproblems actually needed, which is an advantage when the subproblem space is sparse. **Tabulation (bottom-up)** iterates from the smallest subproblems upward, filling a table. It has no recursion overhead and better cache locality (iterating an array sequentially is CPU-cache-friendly). Both have the same asymptotic complexity; tabulation is usually faster in practice and avoids stack-overflow risk on deep recursion.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: fibNaive recomputes fib(3) exponentially many times for large n. fibMemo fixes this with a Map cache — each value is computed once. fibTab eliminates recursion entirely by building from the bottom; using two rolling variables instead of a full O(n) array drops space to O(1). Coin change fills the dp array left-to-right: dp[0]=0 (base), dp[w] tries every coin that fits and takes the minimum — this is classic unbounded knapsack structure.

sections.caption: Coin change tabulation for coins [1,5,10,25], amount 36: each dp[w] builds on earlier results.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Start with recursion, then add a cache.** When facing a DP problem, write the naive recursive solution first — it is the clearest expression of the recurrence. Then add a `memo` Map keyed on the function arguments. This top-down approach is often easier to derive correctly than tabulation. Once it passes, optimise to tabulation (bottom-up) for better constant factors and to avoid stack overflow. The recurrence you found in step 1 is identical — you are just changing the computation order.

items: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has **overlapping subproblems** (same sub-computation needed repeatedly) and **optimal substructure** (global optimum built from subproblem optima).
**Memoisation (top-down)**: add a cache to a recursive solution — compute each subproblem once, store, and return cached results; good when only a subset of subproblems is needed.
**Tabulation (bottom-up)**: fill a dp table iteratively from base cases upward — no recursion overhead, better cache locality, no risk of stack overflow.
The DP approach reduces Fibonacci from O(2ⁿ) to O(n), coin change from exponential to O(n·W), and 0/1 knapsack from O(2ⁿ) to O(n·W) — polynomial time by eliminating redundant work.
Identify DP by asking: (1) can I define a clear recurrence? (2) are subproblems overlapping? (3) does the optimal solution compose from subproblem optima? If all three — it is DP.

quiz.question: What are the two properties that identify a problem as solvable by dynamic programming?
options: Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Sorted input and divide-and-conquer structure
Linear time complexity and constant space
quiz.explanation: DP requires overlapping subproblems (the same subcomputation is needed many times, making caching worthwhile) and optimal substructure (the optimal solution to the problem uses optimal solutions to its subproblems, enabling composition).

quiz.question: Why is the naive recursive Fibonacci implementation O(2^n)?
options: It sorts the recursive calls before executing them
Each call spawns two recursive calls and subproblems are recomputed repeatedly
It uses O(2^n) memory for the call stack
Fibonacci numbers grow exponentially so computation is inherently exponential
quiz.explanation: Each call to fib(n) branches into fib(n-1) and fib(n-2). Without caching, fib(n-2) is computed by both branches, leading to exponential redundancy. fib(40) makes over a billion calls in total.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between memoisation (top-down) and tabulation (bottom-up) DP?
options: Memoisation uses more memory; tabulation uses less
Memoisation starts from the goal and recurses, caching results; tabulation iterates from base cases upward filling a table
Tabulation is only applicable to 1D problems; memoisation works on any dimension
They have different asymptotic complexity
quiz.explanation: Both eliminate redundant computation, but memoisation is top-down (recursive, caches lazily — only computes needed subproblems) while tabulation is bottom-up (iterative, fills the entire dp table from base cases). Asymptotic complexity is the same; tabulation avoids recursion overhead and stack limits.

quiz.question: In the coin change recurrence `dp[w] = 1 + min(dp[w - coin] for each coin)`, what does `dp[0] = 0` represent?
options: It is a sentinel meaning amount 0 is impossible
It is the base case: zero coins are needed to make amount zero
It represents using a coin of value 0
It prevents array index out-of-bounds
quiz.explanation: Amount 0 requires 0 coins — this is the base case that all other dp[w] values build upon. Without dp[0]=0, the recurrence has no foundation and would produce incorrect results (dp[coin] = 1 + dp[0] = 1 is the first derived value).

quiz.question: Why does the 0/1 knapsack bottom-up DP iterate the capacity dimension right-to-left (from W down to weight[i])?
options: To improve cache performance by accessing memory backwards
To ensure each item is considered at most once — right-to-left prevents using the same item's update in the same iteration
To handle negative weights correctly
Because the recurrence only works in reverse order
quiz.explanation: When using a 1D dp array (space-optimised), updating left-to-right would allow item i's value to be added multiple times (unbounded knapsack). Iterating right-to-left ensures dp[w - weight[i]] refers to the state before item i was considered, enforcing the 0/1 constraint.

quiz.question: coinChange([1, 5, 10, 25], 11) — what is the minimum number of coins?
quiz.explanation: 10 + 1 = 11 using 2 coins. The greedy approach (25 too big, try 10: 10+1=11) also works here, but DP is needed for cases where greedy fails (e.g., coins=[1,3,4], amount=6: greedy gives 4+1+1=3 coins, DP gives 3+3=2 coins).

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of the bottom-up coin change DP with `amount=W` and `coins` array of size `k`?
options: O(W)
O(k * W)
O(k log W)
quiz.explanation: The outer loop runs W times (amounts 1 to W), the inner loop runs k times (once per coin). Total: O(k * W). This is the classic 'pseudo-polynomial' complexity — polynomial in the numeric value of W, but exponential in the number of bits representing W.

quiz.question: Which of these problems does NOT have optimal substructure, ruling out standard DP?
options: Longest common subsequence of two strings
Shortest path in a weighted DAG
Longest simple path in a general graph (with cycles)
0/1 Knapsack
quiz.explanation: Shortest path has optimal substructure (sub-paths of shortest paths are shortest paths). But the longest simple path problem does not — a globally longest simple path's sub-paths may not be locally longest simple paths, because avoiding revisiting nodes creates global constraints that break local composability.

quiz.question: You implement fibMemo with a Map cache. What is its time and space complexity?
options: O(2^n) time, O(n) space
O(n) time, O(n) space
O(n log n) time, O(log n) space
O(n) time, O(1) space
quiz.explanation: Each value fib(0) through fib(n) is computed exactly once and cached — n+1 computations total, so O(n) time. The Map stores n+1 entries (O(n) space), and the call stack goes O(n) deep before values start returning. Total space: O(n).

quiz.question: What is the recommended strategy for deriving a DP solution in an interview?
options: Start with the tabulation table immediately and fill it in
Write the brute-force recursive solution first, identify the cache key, add memoisation, then optionally convert to tabulation
Draw the state machine first, then code the transitions
Use greedy first — if it fails, switch to DP
quiz.explanation: The recursive solution directly expresses the recurrence — the hardest intellectual step. Once you have a working recursive solution, adding a memo Map is mechanical. Tabulation reuses the same recurrence in iteration order. Starting with tabulation forces you to derive the recurrence and iteration direction simultaneously, which is harder under interview pressure.
